messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

On the day that changed her life, Mabel was 54 and was cutting grass in the late afternoon light of the family farm. A man she had known for years slipped into her field, pressed her to the dirt and forced her into a violation that left her body and mind trembling. The moment she burst through the fence and sprinted into the scrub, the scent of loam and wet earth still clung to her skin. Years later, the faint smell of soil that the wind carries after a rainstorm in the fields now erupts in her, dragging the night‑time memory of that darkness into her present. In that instant the trigger of earth’s odor pulls her into a cascade of avoidance: she refuses to step foot in the same patch of ground, to be anywhere near the same level of ground in her mind, and she convinces herself that she must think only positive thoughts as a shield. The same smell, however, pulls her to a deeper belief that her life no longer holds meaning—she insists that the event has ruined everything she holds dear. The sense that her body has been dishonored, that the act has tainted her, makes the anniversary of the rape feel like a looming thunderclap. She feels shame in the quiet moments, and the silence in the early dawn on the farm when the machines are idle acts as a reminder that the world has not moved on. These negative appraisals—life not worth living, body shame, contamination—fuel her urge to keep away from any circumstance that reminds her of that day. She avoids being touched, even a casual pat on the shoulder, and she turns her back on any activity that might bring her back into the dark corners of her mind. When she senses even a single hush during the harvest, the absence of sound becomes a trigger that tells her that the threat is again present, and her appraisal that her life is meaningless is reinforced. In the days that followed, Mabel’s coping became a paradox. She told the farmhand who kept the fields together that she “has to think positive thoughts, to keep the bad ideas away.” By refusing to let herself feel anything but optimism, she actually strengthens her sense that the world is cruel and that her life is worthless. The act of forcing a positive frame becomes a trigger in itself: each time she tries to rewrite her thoughts, the memory of that violation flares, and the contamination she feels grows sharper. Her avoidance of being in the dark or being touched keeps her in a loop where the mind stays constantly on high alert, looking for the slightest echo of the event. The more she removes herself from touch and from the smell of earth, the more her appraisal that her body is tainted and her belief that nothing matters are deepened. Now 74, Mabel is still the backbone of the family farm, but she keeps the tractors at a distance, shuns the quiet of the barns, and has stopped allowing her partner, Kofi, to hold her hands during their evening conversations. The isolation has led to restless nights and a sense that she has become a ghost in her own home. When Kofi asked her why she would not let him touch her arm, she could only say, “I feel dirty, and I don’t want to bring that into our lives.” Her fear that the shame will seep into the next generation made her even more reluctant to discuss her trauma, and she finally found herself on the porch one rain‑shrouded afternoon, listening to the distant rumble of the old tractor and realizing she could no longer keep living in the echo of that day. The decision to seek help came after Kofi’s patient insistence that she could not be her own “captive.” Mabel is now afraid that the process will unravel the last thread of control she has held and hopes to regain a sense that her life still has meaning beyond the soil she once feared.
